passage: The panchayat school in their village had its first inter-class debate: should the pond be fenced off? Wasim, fifteen, was against it. At home he practised in front of his mother, Sudha Ammi, who was sorting onions. "Fencing is bad because it's ugly," he began. Ammi raised an eyebrow. "Is that all?" He scowled and went back to his notebook. By evening he had asked the fishermen how many families used the pond and how many children had fallen in last year. He wrote both numbers down. "The other side will say safety," he said. "So I'll say: a fence with a gate, and a rope for rescue." Ammi nodded slowly. "Now that's an argument."

qa.q: Who did Wasim ask about how many families used the pond?
qa.a: He asked the fishermen.

qa.q: Why did Wasim scowl when Ammi asked, "Is that all?"
qa.a: He felt his first argument was being dismissed and was a bit stung, though he also seemed to realise it was weak.

qa.q: What made Wasim's final argument stronger?
qa.a: He gathered real numbers from the fishermen and prepared a fair answer to the safety point instead of just calling the fence ugly.

qa.q: How might a student on the other side see Wasim's fence-with-a-gate idea?
qa.a: They might respect it because it takes their safety worry seriously, which could make the debate feel less like a fight.

grounding: It shows a teen building an argument with evidence and answering the opposing side fairly for a village debate.

passage: Daniel and Freya were paired for the Year 10 debate in Dublin: "Homework should be banned." They had to argue for it, though Freya secretly liked homework. Daniel wanted to open with, "Everyone hates it." Freya shook her head. "That's not evidence. The other team will laugh." They spent Thursday lunch in the library finding a survey on sleep and a report on how much homework actually helped at their age. Freya wrote the other side's best points on sticky notes. "If they say practice matters, we agree, but say it can happen in class." On the day, Daniel's voice shook a little. When a question stumped him, Freya passed him a sticky note. They lost by one vote, but the judge praised their fair rebuttals.

qa.q: Where did Daniel and Freya spend Thursday lunch?
qa.a: They spent it in the library.

qa.q: What does Daniel's shaking voice suggest about how he felt on the day?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous speaking in front of people, even though they had prepared well.

qa.q: Why was writing the other side's points on sticky notes a smart move?
qa.a: It let them plan fair answers in advance, so when a question stumped Daniel, Freya could pass him a ready response.

qa.q: How might Freya feel arguing a side she doesn't personally agree with?
qa.a: She may find it strange at first, but it can help her understand both views and argue more fairly. 🤔

grounding: It shows teens building claims with evidence and preparing to answer counter-arguments fairly in a debate.

passage: The girls' hostel common room became a courtroom on Saturday nights. This week Dilnaz, sixteen, argued that phones should be allowed after lights-out. Usha, the senior monitor, argued against. Dilnaz talked fast. "We need them to call home!" Usha nodded calmly. "You can call home at eight. What's the real reason?" Dilnaz opened her mouth, then stopped. She knew the real reason was watching videos. She took a breath. "Okay. Fair point. But some girls have parents on night shifts. Eight doesn't work for them." The room went quiet. Usha paused. "That's true. Maybe a rule for them, not everyone." Dilnaz sat down, heart still thumping, feeling like she'd lost and won at the same time.

qa.q: What time did Usha say the girls could call home?
qa.a: She said they could call home at eight.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz feel like she had lost and won at the same time?
qa.a: She had to admit her first reason was weak, but her new point about parents on night shifts was strong enough to change Usha's view.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do before the next debate to feel less rushed?
qa.a: She could think through her real reasons and the other side's likely questions in advance, so she leads with her strongest evidence.

qa.q: How might Usha see Dilnaz after this debate?
qa.a: She probably respects her more, because Dilnaz admitted a weak point honestly and then raised a fair argument that Usha had to accept.

grounding: It shows a teen answering a counter-argument honestly and building a fairer claim in a hostel debate.

passage:
Dear Kiran di,
You told me to write after the inter-school debate, so here goes. We lost the semi-final. My motion was 'Homework should be banned in school', and I was FOR it. I had strong feelings but, honestly, weak evidence. I said 'homework causes stress' and the other side asked, 'Where's your source?' I froze.
For the final round, I changed my prep. I found two studies our librarian helped me with, and I wrote the best argument AGAINST me on a card and practised answering it fairly: yes, some practice at home helps with maths, but not three hours a night. The judge wrote 'fair rebuttal' on my sheet! Still lost, but I felt like a real debater.
Miss your tips,
Baljeet

qa.q: What was the motion Baljeet debated?
qa.a: 'Homework should be banned in school', and Baljeet argued for it.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the other side asked for a source?
qa.a: Baljeet froze, embarrassed and caught out by having strong feelings but weak evidence.

qa.q: What did Baljeet change that made the argument stronger?
qa.a: Baljeet found real studies and prepared a fair answer to the best argument against Baljeet's side.

qa.q: How might Kiran di react to this letter?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud that Baljeet learned from losing and used her advice to improve.

passage: So you want to know how I got into debating? Honestly, by losing badly. Class nine, the topic was whether school uniforms should be scrapped. I'm Lavanya, by the way, I'm fifteen. I went up with pure fire: 'Uniforms kill creativity!' Big applause from my friends. Then Sarika from the other school stood up, totally calm. She said, 'That's a fair worry. But here's a survey from our district where students said uniforms reduce teasing about clothes.' She actually repeated my point before answering it! I had nothing to say back. I was so annoyed with myself on the bus home. Now before every debate I write, claim, evidence, and what the other side will say. And I try to answer the way Sarika did.

qa.q: What was the debate topic in class nine?
qa.a: Whether school uniforms should be scrapped.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Lavanya was annoyed at having only passion and no evidence or answer to Sarika's point.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's new preparation method do well?
qa.a: It means backing each claim with evidence and planning a fair response to the other side before speaking.

qa.q: How might Sarika have seen Lavanya's fiery speech?
qa.a: She probably respected the worry behind it, which is why she repeated it fairly before answering with evidence.

grounding: A teenager recalls learning to support claims with evidence and to answer counter-arguments fairly.

passage:
I'm Farida, and I sit next to Chaitanya in Class 10. At the inter-school debate, I watched him in a way I never had before.
The motion was that homework should be banned. Chaitanya was against it. He didn't just shout his opinion. He gave three points, each with a fact: a survey from our own school, a quote from a teacher, and an example from his brother's school.
When the other side said homework causes stress, he nodded. “That's true for too much homework. So let's limit it, not ban it.”
The judges wrote a lot when he spoke. He came second. Afterwards, he said the other team's best point had made him change his closing line.
I don't know how he stayed so calm. I would have argued louder.

qa.q: What was the motion at the debate?
qa.a: That homework should be banned.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya seem to feel when the other side made its point?
qa.a: He seemed calm and open-minded, nodding and taking it seriously.

qa.q: What made Chaitanya's arguments strong?
qa.a: He gave evidence for each point and answered the other side fairly instead of dismissing them.

qa.q: How does Farida see Chaitanya's style of debating?
qa.a: Farida is impressed and a bit puzzled at how calm he stayed.

passage:
Before: In his first school debate in July, Naveen, fourteen, stood up and said uniforms were “stupid and useless,” then sat down. The other side said uniforms reduce show-off pressure. Naveen said, “No, they don't,” and nothing else. He lost badly.
During: Every Tuesday that month, Ms Neelam, the debate coach, made him practise one frame: claim, evidence, reason. “And then say what the other side will say, and answer it.” He hated it at first.
After: In the September final, Naveen argued for school gardens. He gave a survey, an example, and a reason. When the opponent said gardens waste time, he replied, “Some time, yes. But it teaches science and teamwork.” The audience clapped. His team won.

qa.a: Claim, evidence, reason.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the practice frame at first?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and hated it at first.

qa.q: Why did Naveen do better in the September final?

passage:
Aditi, you're preparing for the state debate? Come, let your Leela Nani tell you what I learned the hard way.
When I was seventeen, at a college debate in Mysore, my opponent was a quiet boy from a village school. He spoke slowly, with facts. I thought I could win by making the audience laugh at him. I mocked his accent.
The audience laughed. The judges didn't. I lost.
Afterwards the judge told me, “You didn't answer a single one of his points.”
The next year I faced him again. This time I listened, wrote down his points, and answered each one properly. I won by one mark. And he shook my hand and said, “That was fair.”

qa.q: Where was the college debate?
qa.a: In Mysore.

qa.q: How did young Leela feel after losing the first debate?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and ashamed, realising mocking hadn't worked.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Leela win the next year?
qa.a: Listening to her opponent's points and answering each one properly instead of mocking.

qa.q: How might the village boy have felt when Leela mocked his accent?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and humiliated, even though the judges saw it was unfair.

grounding: A grandmother tells how she learned to answer counter-arguments fairly instead of mocking.

The inter-school debate was on whether homework should be banned. Jaya was speaking against the ban. Then the mic died, and the organisers cut every speech to two minutes.
Jaya threw away half her notes. She kept her strongest claim: homework builds practice. She added one piece of evidence: the study her teacher had shown them.
Kashish, from the other team, argued that too much homework causes stress. Jaya had one minute left.
"My opponent is right that too much homework is harmful," she said. "So the answer isn't a ban. It's less, and better."
The judges wrote something down. Kashish nodded slightly at her across the stage.

passage:
In the Hyderabad school auditorium, the Class 10 debate was on whether uniforms should be compulsory.
Hafsa spoke first, for uniforms. "They reduce showing off. In our school survey, most students said they worry less about clothes."
Lokesh stood up. "But uniforms cost money every year. And they stop us expressing ourselves."
Hafsa listened carefully. She didn't laugh or roll her eyes. When it was her turn, she said, "Lokesh makes a fair point about cost. Maybe the school should provide second-hand uniforms. But the survey shows uniforms help most students feel equal."
Lokesh wrote something on his card. Afterwards he said, "You actually listened. That was annoying."
Hafsa grinned. "Thank you."

qa.q: What did Hafsa say most students said in the survey?
qa.a: They worry less about clothes.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he said "That was annoying"?
qa.a: Lokesh felt a bit frustrated but also respectful, because Hafsa's fair answer was hard to argue with.

qa.q: Which part of Hafsa's reply made her argument stronger?
qa.a: She agreed with Lokesh's fair point on cost, suggested a fix, and then brought it back to her evidence.

qa.q: How might the audience see Hafsa's approach?
qa.a: They may find her more convincing because she listened and answered fairly instead of mocking.

grounding: Two teens debate school uniforms using evidence and fair responses.

passage:
"Okay, practice round. I'm for banning phones in school. Go," said Manoj.
Thomas cleared his throat. "Phones are distracting—"
"No, you're against. Argue against."
"Oh. Right. Phones help us look things up. Some students need them to call parents."
"But students waste time on games."
"That's a claim. Where's your evidence?"
Manoj paused. "Our class teacher said…"
"That's one person's opinion. What about a study?"
Manoj groaned. "You're too good at this."
"You taught me," Thomas laughed. "Now answer my point about parents."
Manoj thought. "Phones stay in lockers, and students can use the office phone."
"Better," Thomas said. "Now it's a real argument."

qa.q: Which side was Thomas supposed to argue?
qa.a: Against banning phones in school.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he groaned?
qa.a: Manoj felt frustrated but also impressed by Thomas's challenge.

qa.q: What could Manoj do before the real debate?
qa.a: Find actual studies or data to support his claim, and prepare answers to likely counter-arguments.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Manoj's first argument?
qa.a: Thomas thinks it's just a claim based on one person's opinion, not solid evidence.

grounding: Two teens practise building claims with evidence and answering counter-arguments.

passage:
I used to think winning a debate meant talking fastest. Our inter-school topic was "Homework should be banned in middle school," and I was against the motion.
My opening had one argument: practice matters. Tanvir, for the motion, said homework causes stress and quoted a survey of students at his school. I laughed and said, "One school doesn't count." The judge frowned. Afterwards she told me I'd attacked the source but ignored the point.
So in the next round I tried it differently. I said, "Tanvir is right that too much homework stresses students. But the problem is the amount, not the idea. Short, useful tasks help." I gave two examples from our class.
We lost the first round and won the second. My name's Gargi, and now I write down the other side's best point before my own.

qa.q: What was the inter-school debate topic?
qa.a: "Homework should be banned in middle school."

qa.q: How do you think Gargi felt when the judge frowned?
qa.a: Gargi likely felt embarrassed and caught out, realising the quick jibe hadn't worked.

qa.q: What changed in Gargi's second round that made the argument stronger?
qa.a: Gargi admitted Tanvir's fair point about stress and then narrowed the claim to the amount of homework, with examples as evidence.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Gargi's second-round reply?
qa.a: Tanvir might feel respected, since his point was taken seriously, even while being challenged.

grounding: Illustrates a teen learning to answer a counter-argument fairly with evidence instead of dismissing it.

passage:
Debate club notes, week 6 (Payal, coach)
Zubin arrives with strong opinions and three facts. Today's motion was "Cities should ban private cars from the centre." Zubin opened well: less pollution, safer streets. When Aisha asked about shopkeepers losing customers, he said, "They'll adjust," and moved on. The room noticed.
In feedback, I asked him to write the strongest version of her point and then answer it. It took him ten minutes. He came back with: shops might lose some customers at first; one city's data showed foot traffic rose after the change; a delivery zone could help.
He was frustrated at first ("Why argue her side for her?"), but the rebuttal was the best he's given. Plan: pair him with Aisha next week, sides reversed.

qa.q: What was today's debate motion?
qa.a: "Cities should ban private cars from the centre."

qa.q: Why did Zubin ask "Why argue her side for her?"
qa.a: Zubin felt frustrated and resistant, thinking it unfair to strengthen his opponent's point.

qa.q: What would you advise Zubin to keep doing after this session?
qa.a: Keep writing the strongest version of the other side's point before answering it, and back each answer with evidence.

qa.q: How might Aisha see Zubin's improved rebuttal?
qa.a: Aisha would likely feel that her question was finally taken seriously, even though he still disagreed.

grounding: Shows a coach helping a teen build claims with evidence and answer counter-arguments fairly.

Wednesday
Class debate: "School phones should be banned." I was for the ban. My argument: phones distract. My evidence: "everyone knows." Great, Afreen, very scientific.
Then Jagdish stood up and said a ban hurts kids who need to call home, like him, because his mother works nights. He also had actual numbers from our own class survey: most people only used phones in breaks. I didn't have anything back. My face went hot.
At home I looked at what I'd written and saw the problem. My claim was too big. So I changed it: "phones switched off in lessons, available in breaks and for calls home." I found two studies Sir had shared about distraction during lessons.
Tomorrow's the second round. I'm scared but I think it's actually a better argument now. And I'm going to thank Jagdish for the survey.

qa.a: His mother works nights, and he needs to be able to call home.

qa.a: Afreen felt embarrassed and caught out; the diary says Afreen's face went hot.

qa.q: What went wrong with Afreen's first argument, and what fixed it?
qa.a: The claim was too big and backed only by "everyone knows"; narrowing the claim and finding real studies fixed it.

qa.q: How might Jagdish react when Afreen thanks him for the survey?
qa.a: Jagdish might feel pleased and respected, seeing that his counter-argument actually changed Afreen's thinking.
